say: Inside your engine, a tiny bolt of lightning strikes thousands of times a minute. And it all starts from a battery with just twelve volts.
But twelve volts can't jump through air. Not even across a gap about one millimeter wide. For that, you need thousands of volts.
So the car uses an ignition coil. It's basically a transformer: a few turns of thick wire, wrapped inside thousands of turns of much thinner wire.
Current flows through the small coil and builds a magnetic field. Then a switch cuts the current off, and the field collapses in a flash.
That collapse surges through the big coil and comes out as a huge spike, often tens of thousands of volts.
The voltage races down to the spark plug and leaps across that tiny gap. The air breaks down, and you get a spark.
That spark lights the squeezed air and fuel at exactly the right moment. Bang. The piston gets pushed, and your car moves.
Many modern cars give every spark plug its own coil, sitting right on top of it. So a four cylinder engine carries four tiny lightning machines.
